claim: IETF draft maps XSS attack scenarios per architecture: BFF blocks token theft and new-token acquisition but leaves 'Proxying Requests via the User's Browser' open; browser-based OAuth client is vulnerable to all scenarios.
quote: Proxying Requests via the User's Browser remains possible because the malicious browser-based code still runs within the application's origin (6.1.4.1.1). ... the use of HttpOnly cookies prevents the attacker from directly accessing the session state (6.1.3.2).

claim: Philippe De Ryck argues avoiding localStorage is the wrong fix: XSS gives full control over application code, so in-memory/worker-hidden tokens are also reachable.
quote: A successful XSS attack gives the attacker full control over your application code. ... In a nutshell, XSS means game over!

claim: FusionAuth: BFF's only remaining XSS vector is request proxying/session riding; the Sept 2025 npm supply-chain compromise showed malicious JS can steal anything JS can read.
quote: The only remaining attack vector is request proxying...the attacker can make requests to your BFF while the user's browser is open. But they can't exfiltrate tokens for offline use.

claim: OWASP: do not store session identifiers in local storage; a single XSS can steal everything in Web Storage; prefer sessionStorage over localStorage when persistence is not needed.
quote: Do not store session identifiers in local storage as the data is always accessible by JavaScript. Cookies can mitigate this risk using the httpOnly flag. ... A single Cross Site Scripting can be used to steal all the data in these objects.

claim: Microsoft MSRC (Nov 2025): XSS is a gateway risk; injected script triggers state-changing requests in the authenticated session; defenses must be layered.
quote: XSS + CSRF ... Injected script triggers state-changing requests in authenticated user session. ... Because attacks are composable, defenses must be layered. Treat XSS as a gateway risk, not a standalone bug.

claim: Pentester walkthrough: with HttpOnly set, XSS still performs authenticated actions via XHR from the user's browser context and reads responses to lift anti-CSRF tokens.
quote: we can still perform this type of attack by defining XHR requests within an XSS payload—this method works because the requests are first loaded through an external script and then sent from the local context of the user's browser. ... Using XHR, an attacker can make the victim perform any action within the application.

claim: web.dev: nonce/hash-based strict CSP with strict-dynamic blocks untrusted inline scripts and javascript: URIs, but does not stop injections into a nonced script body, dynamically created script locations, AngularJS template injection, or eval sinks.
quote: It blocks untrusted inline scripts like inline event handlers or javascript: URIs. ... If you nonce a script, but there's an injection directly into the body or the src parameter of that <script> element.

claim: Google/ACM CCS 2016 internet-scale study: 94.68% of script-limiting CSP policies were ineffective; allowlist-based CSP is largely bypassable, motivating nonce + strict-dynamic.
quote: 94.68% of policies that attempt to limit script execution are ineffective, and ... 99.34% of hosts with CSP use policies that offer little to no benefit against XSS.

claim: Trusted Types enforces safe DOM manipulation at the sink level; Safari 26 (Sept 2025) and Firefox (Feb 2026) shipped it, reaching Baseline; a no-op policy still provides false security.
quote: Firefox completed the picture in February 2026, at which point Trusted Types reached Baseline status ... Any value that reaches a sink must have passed through your policy first, or the browser throws a TypeError.

claim: MDN: require-trusted-types-for disallows raw strings at DOM XSS injection sinks, requiring values produced by a Trusted Types policy.
quote: The HTTP Content-Security-Policy (CSP) require-trusted-types-for directive instructs user agents to control the data passed to DOM XSS sink functions.

claim: Duende BFF: browser never sees tokens, server-side session state, server can forcibly end sessions, built-in CSRF protection via a required custom header; session hijacking is acknowledged as hard to fully prevent.
quote: Server-side only — browser never sees tokens ... Server can forcibly end sessions ... just the fact that this header must be present is enough to protect the BFF from CSRF attacks ... Session hijacking...Right now, it's very difficult to completely protect against this type of attack

claim: Auth0: BFF shifts the security boundary rather than eliminating it; tokens in memory are as reachable as tokens in localStorage; the trade is XSS token theft for a more constrained CSRF surface.
quote: BFF shifts the security boundary. It doesn't eliminate it. ... Tokens in localStorage, sessionStorage, or even JavaScript memory are all reachable by malicious scripts. ... You're trading one attack vector (XSS-based token theft) for a different, more constrained one (CSRF).

claim: HN thread on Keycloak/Angular/BFF: contrarian commenter horsawlarway argues httpOnly cookies only add marginal complexity for an attacker who can script the page directly; TobbenTM defends BFF as keeping session tokens server-side.
quote: All it does is add a marginal level of complexity... still completely hacked.

claim: HttpOnly cookies are still automatically attached to same-origin fetch/XHR issued by JavaScript — the mechanical basis of session riding.
quote: Cookies marked with HttpOnly are still automatically included in same-origin requests made by JavaScript (such as fetch or XMLHttpRequest calls), ensuring your application functions normally while remaining protected.

claim: Duende's marketing framing: with BFF, an XSS-compromised browser app carries no risk of access-token theft.
quote: If the browser based application is compromised, for example with XSS attacks, there is no risk of the attacker stealing the access tokens.

claim: HN commenter unscaled: HttpOnly cookies are genuinely better security-wise; storing refresh tokens in local storage is only for low-security use cases.
quote: HttpOnly cookies ARE better in terms of security. Storing Refresh Tokens in local storage is only recommended for low-security use cases...

claim: Chrome docs: Trusted Types blocks risky injection points such as .innerHTML from accepting unvalidated string values.
quote: blocking risky injection points (like .innerHTML) from using unvalidated string values
